'''Solomon Lefschetz''' {{Post-nominals|country=||list=[[Foreign Member of the Royal Society|ForMemRS]]}} ({{langx|ru|Соломо́н Ле́фшец}}; 3 September 1884 – 5 October 1972) was a Russian-born American [[mathematician]] who did fundamental work on [[algebraic topology]], its applications to [[algebraic geometry]], and the theory of non-linear [[ordinary differential equation]]s.<ref name="mathgene"/><ref name="frs"/><ref>{{cite journal|author=Markus, L.|title=Solomon Lefschetz: An appreciation in memoriam|journal=Bull. Amer. Math. Soc.|year=1973|volume=79|issue=4|pages=663–680|url=http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.bams/1183534736|doi=10.1090/s0002-9904-1973-13256-2|doi-access=free|archive-date=2020-06-26|access-date=2012-07-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200626043411/https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.bams/1183534736|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="mactutor">{{MacTutor Biography|id=Lefschetz}}</ref>

==Life==
He was born in [[Moscow]], the son of Alexander Lefschetz and his wife Sarah or Vera Lifschitz, both [[Russian-Jewish]] traders who used to travel around Europe and the Middle East (since they held [[Ottoman Empire|Ottoman]] passports).<ref name="mactutor"/> Thereafter, the family moved to [[Paris]] and he was educated there in [[engineering]] at the [[École Centrale Paris]] but emigrated to the US in 1905.

He was badly injured in an industrial accident in 1907, losing both hands.<ref>{{Google books |id=dZh2SnbSxAcC |title=Mathematical Apocrypha: Stories and Anecdotes of Mathematicians and the Mathematical |page=148 }}</ref> He moved towards mathematics, receiving a [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in algebraic geometry from [[Clark University]] in Worcester, Massachusetts in 1911.<ref name="thesis-lefschetz-1911">{{cite thesis |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/301745812 |title=On the existence of LocI with given singularities |date=1911 |publisher=[[Clark University]] |type=Ph.D. |last=Lefschetz |first=Solomon |id={{ProQuest|301745812}} |url-access=subscription |oclc=245921866 |archive-date=2023-03-17 |access-date=2022-05-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230317113654/https://www.proquest.com/docview/301745812/ |url-status=live }}</ref> He then took positions at the [[University of Nebraska–Lincoln|University of Nebraska]] and [[University of Kansas]], moving to [[Princeton University]] in 1924, where he was soon given a permanent position. He remained there until 1953.

In the application of topology to algebraic geometry, he followed the work of [[Charles Émile Picard]], whom he had heard lecture in Paris at the [[École Centrale Paris]]. He proved theorems on the topology of [[hyperplane]] sections of [[algebraic varieties]], which provide a basic inductive tool (these are now seen as allied to [[Morse theory]], though a [[Lefschetz pencil]] of hyperplane sections is a more subtle system than a Morse function because hyperplanes intersect each other). The [[Picard–Lefschetz theory|Picard–Lefschetz formula]] in the theory of [[vanishing cycle]]s is a basic tool relating the [[degeneracy (mathematics)|degeneration]] of families of varieties with 'loss' of topology, to [[monodromy]]. He was an Invited Speaker of the [[International Congress of Mathematicians|ICM]] in 1920 in Strasbourg.<ref>{{cite book|chapter-url=http://www.mathunion.org/ICM/ICM1920/Main/icm1920.0300.0307.ocr.pdf|pages=300–307|year=1921|title=Compte rendu du Congrès international des mathématiciens tenu à Strasbourg du 22 au 30 Septembre 1920|chapter=''Quelques remarques sur la multiplication complexe'' by S. Lefschetz|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171029065313/http://www.mathunion.org/ICM/ICM1920/Main/icm1920.0300.0307.ocr.pdf|archive-date=2017-10-29}}</ref> His book ''L'analysis situs et la géométrie algébrique'' from 1924, though opaque foundationally given the current technical state of [[homology theory]], was in the long term very influential (one could say that it was one of the sources for the eventual proof of the [[Weil conjectures]], through [[Séminaire de Géométrie Algébrique du Bois Marie#SGA 7|SGA 7]]  also for the study of [[Picard group]]s of [[Zariski surface]]). In 1924 he was awarded the [[Bôcher Memorial Prize]] for his work in [[mathematical analysis]]. He was elected to the United States [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 1925 and the [[American Philosophical Society]] in 1929.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Solomon Lefschetz |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/solomon-lefschetz-wyadsg/ |access-date=2023-07-20 |website=www.nasonline.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=APS Member History |url=https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=Solomon+Lefschetz&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced |access-date=2023-07-20 |website=search.amphilsoc.org |archive-date=2023-07-20 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230720152257/https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=Solomon+Lefschetz&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced |url-status=live }}</ref>

The [[Lefschetz fixed-point theorem]], now a basic result of topology, was developed by him in papers from 1923 to 1927, initially for [[manifold]]s. Later, with the rise of [[cohomology theory]] in the 1930s, he contributed to the [[intersection number]] approach (that is, in cohomological terms, the ring structure) via the [[cup product]] and duality on manifolds. His work on topology was summed up in his monograph ''[http://www.ams.org/online_bks/coll27/ Algebraic Topology]'' (1942). From 1944 he worked on [[differential equation]]s.

He was editor of the ''[[Annals of Mathematics]]'' from 1928 to 1958. During this time, the ''Annals'' became an increasingly well-known and respected journal, and Lefschetz played an important role in this.<ref name=NAS>{{Cite web |url = https://www.ma.utexas.edu/users/dafr/M382C/Readings/slefschetz.pdf |title = Solomon Lefschetz 1884–1972 |first1=Phillip |last1=Griffiths|author-link1=Phillip Griffiths|first2= Donald|last2= Spencer|author-link2=Donald Spence|first3=George|last3=Whitehead| author-link3=George W. Whitehead |date = 1992 |publisher = National Academy of Sciences |url-status = dead |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20141222053811/https://www.ma.utexas.edu/users/dafr/M382C/Readings/slefschetz.pdf |archive-date = 2014-12-22 }}</ref>

In 1945 he travelled to Mexico for the first time, where he joined the Institute of Mathematics at the [[National University of Mexico]] as a visiting professor. He visited frequently for long periods, and during 1953–1966 he spent most of his winters in Mexico City.<ref name=NAS /> He played an important role in the foundation of mathematics in Mexico, and sent several students back to Princeton. His students included Emilio Lluis, [[José Adem]], [[Samuel Gitler Hammer|Samuel Gitler]], [[Santiago López de Medrano]], [[Francisco Javier González-Acuña]] and Alberto Verjovsky.<ref name=mexico/>

Lefschetz came out of retirement in 1958, because of the launch of [[Sputnik]], to augment the mathematical component of [[Glenn L. Martin Company]]'s [[Research Institute for Advanced Studies]] (RIAS) in Baltimore, Maryland. His team became the world's largest group of mathematicians devoted to research in [[nonlinear differential equation]]s.<ref>Allen, K. N. (1988, January). Undaunted genius. ''Clark News'', '''11'''(1), p. 9.</ref>  The RIAS mathematics group stimulated the growth of nonlinear differential equations through conferences and publications. He left RIAS in 1964 to form the Lefschetz Center for Dynamical Systems at [[Brown University]], Providence, Rhode Island.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://sites.brown.edu/dynamical-systems/|title=Lefschetz Center for Dynamical Systems|website=sites.brown.edu}}</ref>
